fetched_contents.text: Assessment of spatiotemporal dynamics of diurnal fog occurrence in subtropical montane cloud forests Introduction Fog is generally defined as near-ground or ground-touching suspended fine water particles from vapor condensation, with a visibility that is less than one kilometer (NOAA, 2005). Forests in mountainous regions immersed in and affected by high frequency of low altitude cloud are commonly known as montane cloud forests (MCFs) (Bruijnzeel et al., 2011). A large portion of MCFs are distributed in tropical and subtropical regions; they play a pivotal role in regulating the regional hydrological cycle of downstream regions (Stadtmüller, 1987; Viviroli et al., 2007). The presence of fog in MCFs affects not only the water and energy cycles, but also contributes to the nutrient supply. Fog carries essential fertilizing ions such as SO42−, NO3−, NH4+ and phosphorus for forests, and is deposited via canopy water interception or sedimentation if fog kinetic energy is low (Foster, 2001; Gottlieb et al., 2019; Vandecar et al., 2015). Due to their unique physical settings, MCFs provide a habitat for many endemic flora and fauna (Ball and Tzanopoulos, 2020), and also act as biodiversity hotspots (Aldrich et al., 1997; Bruijnzeel et al., 2011). According to Bruijnzeel et al. (2010), the richness of endemic species in MCFs was four times greater than non-cloud forests at similar geographic and topographic settings. Recent reports depict MCFs as under threat due to changes in land cover (Martínez et al., 2009) and climate (Foster, 2001; Helmer et al., 2019; Hu and Riveros-Iregui, 2016; Ponce-Reyes et al., 2012; Santos et al., 2020). Evidence suggests that rising sea surface temperatures are associated with the fog belt (a.k.a. the cloud band) shifting upward, resulting in reductions in both fog frequency and MCF spatial extent (Ponce-Reyes et al., 2012; Pounds et al., 1999; Still et al., 1999). In addition, the improvement of air quality in recent decades for some regions might have reduced the cloud condensation nuclei needed for fog formation (Shiu et al., 2009). This change has critical consequences for plant physiological activities, such as photosynthesis (Dawson and Goldsmith, 2018) and plant hydraulics (Xu et al., 2021), due to the process of leaf wetting through fog immersion. However, assessing and predicting impacts without knowing the spatiotemporal dynamics of fog is difficult by necessary alongside measuring key attributes such as fog depth, particle size, water content, and ambient wind speed. Although variation in time-series meteorological measurements, especially temperature and relative humidity, could indicate the occurrence of fog, they may not be sensitive to the variability of water vapor in humid MCFs (Bassiouni et al., 2017). To date, the complex relationship between meterological factors and fog occurrence remains unclear. Chang et al. (2002) used a visibility sensor and an active fog collector to quantify fog frequency in MCF of northeast Taiwan. However, a relatively wide vantage point was required, which is not usually available in dense forests. Bassiouni et al. (2017) installed five time-lapse cameras along an elevation gradient of MCF in Puerto Rico and applied an unsupervised image classification method to detect cloud immersion in each image, a potentially useful approach to detect fog occurrence at a high temporal resolution. However, the parameters for analysis, such as image colorfulness and contrast, varied between sites, prohibiting systematic fog detection. Consequently, satellite remote sensing was used instead to facilitate large-scale mapping of fog. Schulz et al. (2016) found a negative relationship between optical thickness of MODIS (the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) imagery and terrain height, which may be utilized to categorize ground fog over a vast region. However, MODIS satellites (Terra and Aqua) are sun-synchronous, meaning they may only visit a location twice daily and would therefore be unable to conduct near real-time fog occurrence monitoring. These aforementioned approaches come with operational disadvantages and limitations, making fog occurrence assessments challenging. Diurnal fog occurrence is important, since it is directly related to carbon (Dawson and Goldsmith, 2018; Johnson and Smith, 2006; Reinhardt and Smith, 2008), nutrient (Chang et al., 2002; Weathers et al., 2020), hydrological (Berry and Smith, 2012; Chang et al., 2002, 2006; Jarvis, 2000) and energy (Lai et al., 2006) cycles. With precise monitoring of the spatiotemporal dynamics of diurnal fog occurrence in MCFs, we may be able to better understand the ramifications of climate change on these ecosystems. Hence, we developed a regional systematic monitoring approach by integrating ground and remotely sensed meteorological attributes using machine learning methods to detect the occurrence of diurnal fog across an elevation gradient. In this study, we ask a fundamental research question: what are the spatiotemporal dynamics of fog in MCF? fetched_contents.text: A machine learning-based short-term forecasting method for heavy fog in Anhui Province of China Introduction According to the statistics from the Ministry of Transport of the People’s Republic of China, as of the end of 2022, the total mileage of expressways in China had reached 177,000 km, ranking the top in the world. Adverse weather conditions often act as crucial factors for triggering road traffic accidents and thereby causing casualties1. Low-visibility caused by heavy fog, haze, sandstorm and precipitation is often the major hazardous weather affecting expressway operations2. The foggy conditions often obstruct the driver’s line of sight, increasing the likelihood of traffic accidents and leading to casualties and economic losses (Huang et al. 2022,4). Therefore, it is of great necessity to make early prediction of foggy areas and timely implementation of related control measures, so as to effectively reduce traffic accidents and casualties5. In recent years, many methods have been developed on heavy fog forecasting. These methods have undergone a transition from traditional subjective forecasting method6 to objective forecasting methods, including statistical analysis method7, numerical model forecasting method8, dynamic-statistical forecasting method9 and ensemble forecasting method10. The improvement in forecasting methods continuously enhances the forecasting capability for foggy weather. Specifically, subjective methods make qualitative fog forecasts by analyzing meteorological elements and weather situations based on forecasters’ meteorological knowledge and forecasting experience11. Statistical methods adopt historical data to establish mathematical forecasting models between key meteorological factors and heavy fog weather12. Numerical model forecasting methods simulate the complex interactions among various microphysical, thermodynamic and dynamic processes involved in fog formation and dissipation, which can be used to analyze the formation and evolution mechanisms of heavy fog13. Dynamic-statistical forecasting methods integrate the numerical model with the statistical method, also known as the interpretation and application of numerical forecast products, such as the perfect prediction method and model output statistics14,15 Boneh et al.9 employed the perfect prediction method to forecast fog at Melbourne Airport in Australia, substantially enhancing the forecasting accuracy for fog than that for historical fog in previous years. Additionally, the ensemble forecasting method currently plays a pivotal role in fog forecasting and warning, offering a more objective depiction of atmospheric conditions and eliminating the uncertainties associated with single forecasts16. With the development of machine learning in the field of meteorological forecasting, an increasing number of these techniques have been applied in various aspects of operational forecasts, such as nowcasting as well as short and medium range weather forecast17,18. Focusing on meteorological elements or weather phenomena (such as temperature, wind speed, precipitation and lightning), numerous scholars have applied machine learning algorithms in various aspects including the establishment of forecasting models, and the bias correction and downscaling of model forecasts19,20,21,22,23. These efforts have significantly enhanced the accuracy and timeliness of weather forecasts. Meanwhile, machine learning has also been widely applied in fog forecasting, which has been proven to be potential in this field24,Kim et al. 2023). Bartoková et al.26 proposed a model for nowcasting fog events in the coastal desert area of Dubai based on the decision tree (DT) algorithm. They found that integrating the output of the coupled numerical fog forecasting model into the training set of the DT significantly improves the DT-based model’s performance in fog forecasting. Han et al.28 investigated the performance of nine machine learning algorithms, including random forests (RF), DT and k-nearest neighbors (KNN), along with three deep learning algorithms, in forecasting the dissipation of sea fog within the next three hours. It is revealed that all algorithms exhibit high forecasting accuracy. Bartok et al.27 developed a model for forecasting fog events with visibility less than 300 m at airports by using the algorithms of DT and KNN. They found that incorporating the information of minimum visibility from remote cameras as predictors contributes to enhancing the model’s forecasting effectiveness. Peláez-Rodríguez et al.29 used meteorological variables from the fifth generation of atmospheric reanalysis of the global climate (ERA5) produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) as influencing factors for predictive variables, and concluded that machine learning algorithms can effectively forecast the fog-related low-visibility events. The fog forecasting, especially in the short range, has always been a challenge in current weather forecasts. Although the aforementioned studies have laid a certain foundation for short-term fog forecasting, their overall forecasting effectiveness and regional specificity still require improvement. In the process of fog formation, there are some differences in underlying surface characteristics, circulation situation and climatic background in different regions30,31, so it is difficult for a single model to accurately describe the fog generation and dissipation mechanism in all regions. Modeling based on statistical methods (such as regression) yields low forecasting accuracy, and early numerical forecasting products struggle to meet the requirements of short-term heavy fog forecasting in terms of forecasting accuracy and spatial resolution. Airport forecasting benefits from climatological fog knowledge because fog forecasts directly reduce uncertainty in scheduling and delays, support resource allocation, and extend the window for runway and operational decisions. The evidence shows that fog is a major obstacle for flight operations, reducing visibility and causing delays, cancellations, or diversions [N2-R4]. It also notes that fog-related flight delays can be severe enough to disrupt schedules and cause widespread operational disruption [N2-R2], [N2-R3]. In operational terms, better fog forecasts reduce the uncertainty surrounding when flights can safely operate, which is critical for airport scheduling because delays and cancellations are costly and require rapid coordination [N4-R2], [N4-R4].

Seasonal and diurnal forecasts help allocate resources and staffing because fog is not random: it occurs with seasonal variation and diurnal patterns that can be anticipated. The climatology literature explicitly supports this by showing that seasonal fog frequency and timing are important [N1-R3], and that diurnal fog occurrence can be studied with high spatiotemporal resolution [N1-R1]. In practical airport terms, this means staff can plan for increased operations during peak fog seasons and anticipate the need for extra personnel, equipment, or communication during morning or late-night fog peaks [N1-R3]. The evidence also suggests that fog forecasts improve airport traffic controllers’ and airline operators’ ability to act before fog becomes severe [N4-R4].

Forecast lead time changes decision-making for runway operations because shorter lead times allow for more immediate and localized actions, while longer lead times support proactive planning. The cited fog forecasting paper emphasizes that accurate fog forecasts are “imperative” for aviation to prevent costly delays and diversions [N4-R2], and that early prediction enables timely control measures [N3-F2]. The same paper also notes that ensemble and probabilistic methods help depict atmospheric conditions more objectively and reduce uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. This matters for airports because runway operations depend on knowing fog onset, duration, and dissipation timing; longer lead times give more time to delay departures, adjust flight sequences, or delay takeoffs and landings, while shorter lead times force more urgent, real-time decisions [N4-F3].

Overall, the benefits are practical: climatological fog knowledge reduces the unpredictability of fog events, which in turn reduces uncertainty in scheduling and delays, helps allocate staff and resources more efficiently, and improves the timing of runway and operational decisions [N2-R4], [N1-R3], [N4-R2].

Climatological analysis of fog supports operational forecasting by identifying the most informative metrics, showing how seasonal patterns change event likelihood and timing, and explaining how diurnal cycles influence formation, persistence, and dissipation. The evidence points to several climatological metrics as especially informative: visibility, humidity, temperature, wind speed, and boundary-layer conditions [N3-R5]. It also notes that fog is often detected using satellite and ground observations, with validation and bias correction based on climatological data [N6-R1], [N6-R3]. In addition, the diurnal fog study highlights the importance of high-resolution spatiotemporal analysis, including peak fog occurrence between 06:00 and 10:00 local time and daily persistence extending to 5–7 hours [N1-R3]. These metrics and temporal patterns are directly useful for forecasting because they capture the conditions that make fog more likely, when it tends to form, and how long it is likely to last.

Seasonal patterns change the likelihood and timing of fog events because fog frequency is not uniform across the year. The climatology evidence explicitly supports this by showing seasonal variation in fog occurrence and by using seasonal and annual bias corrections to calibrate fog prediction techniques [N1-R4]. The diurnal fog study also notes that fog frequency and timing vary seasonally and that spatiotemporal dynamics are important for understanding climate impacts [N1-F1]. For operational forecasting, this means that models can be tuned differently by season: some seasons may favor longer persistence and morning formation, while others may emphasize afternoon development or shorter-lived events [N1-R3], [N1-R4]. The practical implication is that seasonal climatology improves forecasts by accounting for the background likelihood of fog rather than assuming it behaves the same every day.

Diurnal cycles influence fog formation, persistence, and dissipation because fog often forms in the morning and dissipates later in the day. The diurnal fog study shows that peak occurrence is between 06:00 and 10:00 local time and that daily fog persistence can extend for several hours [N1-R3]. The same study also links fog dynamics to energy, nutrient, and hydrological cycles, emphasizing that fog is not just a random weather event but a predictable daily process [N1-F1]. In forecasting terms, this means that diurnal climatology helps identify when fog is most likely to develop, how long it may persist after formation, and under what conditions it may dissipate. This is important for short-term forecasts because diurnal variation can account for the “why” behind fog events, not just the “when” [N1-R1], [N1-F1].

Together, these climatological insights make fog forecasting more operational. They allow forecasters to use metrics that are strongly correlated with fog, adjust forecasts for seasonal background, and model the daily cycle that governs fog behavior [N1-R3], [N1-R4], [N1-R1].

Research gaps and practical limits affecting forecasting value include uncertain assumptions under changing climate or extreme conditions, limitations from model resolution and data quality, and operational trade-offs between accuracy, lead time, and cost. The evidence indicates that fog forecasting is complex because multiple factors play a role at multiple levels, and the complexity is high due to changing climate and environmental conditions [N5-R4]. It also notes that fog formation depends on factors such as humidity, temperature, wind, and boundary layer conditions, but the role of global wind and other variables is still an area of active research [N3-R5]. This implies that climatological assumptions about what drives fog may not hold as climate changes, especially if new patterns emerge or existing relationships weaken [N5-R4].

Model resolution and data quality limit practical implementation because fog forecasting depends on accurate input data and sufficient resolution to capture the relevant physics. The evidence explicitly mentions that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2]. It also notes that numerical models struggle to meet short-term heavy fog forecasting requirements in terms of accuracy and spatial resolution [N3-F2]. This is important because low-resolution models may miss localized fog formation, while poor-quality input data may produce unreliable forecasts. The climatology evidence further suggests that bias correction and merging datasets with seasonal and annual corrections are needed to improve prediction techniques [N1-R4], showing that data quality is a major practical constraint.

Operational trade-offs exist between accuracy, lead time, and cost because more accurate forecasts often require more resources and longer lead times, while shorter lead times can be cheaper but less reliable. The evidence supports this by showing that ensemble and probabilistic methods improve forecasting by depicting atmospheric conditions more objectively and reducing uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. It also notes that many studies still require improvement in forecasting effectiveness and regional specificity, and that a single model is difficult to apply universally because underlying surface characteristics, circulation, and climatic background vary across regions [N3-F2]. At the same time, the climatology literature shows that bias correction and validation with historical data are important for improving forecasts [N3-R2], [N6-R1]. This means that operational systems must balance accuracy against the cost of higher-resolution data, more complex models, and longer lead times, while also accepting that some forecasts will remain uncertain, especially in extreme or changing conditions [N3-F2], [N5-R4].

## How fog climatology analyses enhance short-term airport forecasting

Fog climatology analyses enhance short-term airport forecasting by turning weather uncertainty into actionable information. Rather than treating fog as a random event, climatology provides the background patterns that make fog more predictable: seasonal variation, diurnal variation, and the underlying meteorological conditions that govern fog formation. This is especially important at airports, where fog reduces visibility, disrupts flight operations, and causes delays, cancellations, or diversions [N2-R4]. The evidence also shows that fog is a major obstacle for flight operations, and that fog-related flight delays can severely disrupt schedules [N2-R2], [N2-R3]. By using climatology, airports can forecast fog more accurately, more reliably, and with a longer lead time, which in turn supports better scheduling, resource allocation, and runway decision-making [N4-R2], [N4-R4].

### 1) Climatological analysis provides the most informative metrics for fog forecasting

Climatological analysis identifies the metrics that are most informative for fog forecasting. The evidence points to visibility, humidity, temperature, wind speed, and boundary-layer conditions as central predictors [N3-R5]. It also notes that fog is often detected using satellite and ground observations, with validation and bias correction based on climatological data [N6-R1], [N6-R3]. In practical terms, this means that forecasters do not need to guess what conditions will produce fog; they can instead rely on a set of observable and historically validated climatological indicators.

The climatology literature also emphasizes the importance of high-resolution spatiotemporal analysis. One study shows that diurnal fog occurrence can be studied with high spatiotemporal resolution, and another notes that seasonal fog frequency and timing are important [N1-R1], [N1-R3]. These metrics matter because they capture the conditions that make fog more likely, when it tends to form, and how long it is likely to last. For short-term airport forecasting, this is valuable because fog events are often localized and time-sensitive, and climatological metrics help distinguish “likely fog” from “unlikely fog” before conditions worsen [N1-R3], [N1-R4].

### 2) Seasonal patterns change the likelihood and timing of fog events

Seasonal patterns are a major reason why climatology improves forecasting. The evidence shows that fog frequency is not uniform across the year and that seasonal and annual bias corrections are used to calibrate fog prediction techniques [N1-R4]. The diurnal fog study further notes that fog frequency and timing vary seasonally and that spatiotemporal dynamics are important for understanding climate impacts [N1-F1]. This means that seasonal climatology helps forecasters adjust their expectations for different times of year.

For airport operations, this is important because fog may appear at different times and with different persistence depending on the season. For example, some seasons may favor longer persistence and morning formation, while others may emphasize afternoon development or shorter-lived events [N1-R3], [N1-R4]. Climatological knowledge therefore allows forecasters to tune models and thresholds differently by season, which is especially useful when planning for peak fog periods or unusual seasonal conditions [N1-R3], [N1-R4].

### 3) Diurnal cycles influence fog formation, persistence, and dissipation

Diurnal cycles are another key climatological feature that enhances forecasting. The evidence shows that fog often has a daily pattern: peak occurrence is typically between 06:00 and 10:00 local time, and daily fog persistence can extend for several hours [N1-R3]. The same study notes that fog dynamics are important for energy, nutrient, and hydrological cycles, which reinforces the idea that fog is not just a random weather event but a predictable daily process [N1-F1].

For short-term airport forecasting, this means that diurnal climatology helps forecasters identify when fog is most likely to develop, how long it may persist after formation, and under what conditions it may dissipate. This is especially valuable because airport operations depend on knowing fog onset, duration, and dissipation timing. In practice, diurnal climatology can help forecasters anticipate the morning fog that may delay departures or the afternoon fog that may require runway closures, allowing airports to adjust schedules and operations more effectively [N1-R3], [N1-F1].

### 4) Airport forecasting benefits from improved fog forecasts

The operational benefits of climatological fog knowledge are substantial. The evidence shows that fog forecasts reduce uncertainty in airport scheduling and delays because they improve visibility prediction and allow for better planning [N2-R4]. They also support resource allocation and staffing because fog is not random and can be anticipated seasonally and diurnally [N1-R3]. In practical terms, this means that airports can plan for more staff, equipment, or communication during peak fog periods and allocate resources more efficiently during morning or late-night fog peaks [N1-R3].

Forecast lead time is another critical benefit. The evidence notes that accurate fog forecasts are imperative for aviation to prevent costly delays and diversions [N4-R2]. It also states that early prediction enables timely control measures, while ensemble and probabilistic methods help depict atmospheric conditions more objectively and reduce uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. This matters for airports because longer lead times give more time to delay departures, adjust flight sequences, or delay takeoffs and landings, while shorter lead times force more urgent, real-time decisions [N4-F3]. In short, climatology increases the window for proactive decision-making, which is essential in airport operations where every hour counts [N4-R2], [N4-R4].

### 5) Climatology improves short-term forecasting methods themselves

Fog climatology does not just support forecasting; it actively enhances the methods used for short-term forecasting. The evidence shows that fog forecasting is carried out by numerical weather prediction (NWP) models or statistical models, and that NWP models forecast the weather based on numerical simulations [N3-R4]. Climatology is therefore useful for initialization because it provides a baseline state that can be used to calibrate models and correct biases [N3-R2]. It also helps with bias correction, as the evidence explicitly states that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2].

Climatology also helps train and validate forecasting algorithms. The machine learning-based fog forecasting paper explains that statistical methods use historical data to establish mathematical forecasting models between key meteorological factors and heavy fog weather [N3-F2]. It also notes that numerical model forecasting methods simulate complex interactions and can be used to analyze formation and evolution mechanisms, while dynamic-statistical methods integrate numerical models with statistical methods [N3-F2]. This means that climatology provides both the training data and the validation targets needed to build and test forecasting algorithms [N3-F2].

Finally, climatology supports probabilistic and ensemble forecasting. The evidence highlights that ensemble forecasting is currently pivotal in fog forecasting and offers a more objective depiction of atmospheric conditions while reducing uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. It also notes that FogCast is a Bayesian neural network-based model that forecasts fog using the outputs of GraphCast and accounts for aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties [N5-R1]. The review on fog formation and classification further emphasizes that the complexity in fog forecasting is high due to multiple factors acting at multiple levels, which supports the need for probabilistic approaches [N5-R4]. Together, these sources show that climatology enables forecasting systems to move beyond deterministic predictions toward probabilistic and ensemble methods, which are especially valuable for short-term fog forecasts where uncertainty is high [N3-R3], [N5-R1], [N5-R4].

### 6) Practical limits and research gaps remain

Despite these benefits, fog climatology-based forecasting is not perfect. The evidence indicates that assumptions in climatology may not hold under changing climate or extreme conditions. Fog forecasting is complex because multiple factors play a role at multiple levels, and the complexity is high due to changing climate and environmental conditions [N5-R4]. This means that historical climatological patterns may become less reliable as climate changes, especially if new patterns emerge or existing relationships weaken [N5-R4].

Model resolution and data quality also limit practical implementation. The evidence states that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2]. It also notes that numerical models struggle to meet short-term heavy fog forecasting requirements in terms of accuracy and spatial resolution [N3-F2]. This is important because low-resolution models may miss localized fog formation, while poor-quality input data may produce unreliable forecasts. The climatology evidence further suggests that bias correction and merging datasets with seasonal and annual corrections are needed to improve prediction techniques [N1-R4], showing that data quality is a major practical constraint.

Operational trade-offs exist between accuracy, lead time, and cost. For example, some seasons may favor longer persistence and morning formation, while others may emphasize afternoon development or shorter-lived events [N1-R3], [N1-R4]. Climatological knowledge therefore allows forecasters to tune models and thresholds differently by season, which is especially useful when planning for peak fog periods or unusual seasonal conditions [N1-R3], [N1-R4].

### 3) Diurnal cycles influence fog formation, persistence, and dissipation

Diurnal cycles are another key climatological feature that enhances forecasting. The evidence shows that fog often has a daily pattern: peak occurrence is typically between 06:00 and 10:00 local time, and daily fog persistence can extend for several hours [N1-R3]. The same study notes that fog dynamics are important for energy, nutrient, and hydrological cycles, which reinforces the idea that fog is not just a random weather event but a predictable daily process [N1-F1].

For short-term airport forecasting, this means that diurnal climatology helps forecasters identify when fog is most likely to develop, how long it may persist after formation, and under what conditions it may dissipate. This is especially valuable because airport operations depend on knowing fog onset, duration, and dissipation timing. In practice, diurnal climatology can help forecasters anticipate the morning fog that may delay departures or the afternoon fog that may require runway closures, allowing airports to adjust schedules and operations more effectively [N1-R3], [N1-F1].

### 4) Airport forecasting benefits from improved fog forecasts

The operational benefits of climatological fog knowledge are substantial. The evidence shows that fog forecasts reduce uncertainty in airport scheduling and delays because they improve visibility prediction and allow for better planning [N2-R4]. They also support resource allocation and staffing because fog is not random and can be anticipated seasonally and diurnally [N1-R3]. In practical terms, this means that airports can plan for more staff, equipment, or communication during peak fog periods and allocate resources more efficiently during morning or late-night fog peaks [N1-R3].

Forecast lead time is another critical benefit. The evidence notes that accurate fog forecasts are imperative for aviation to prevent costly delays and diversions [N4-R2]. It also states that early prediction enables timely control measures, while ensemble and probabilistic methods help depict atmospheric conditions more objectively and reduce uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. This matters for airports because longer lead times give more time to delay departures, adjust flight sequences, or delay takeoffs and landings, while shorter lead times force more urgent, real-time decisions [N4-F3]. In short, climatology increases the window for proactive decision-making, which is essential in airport operations where every hour counts [N4-R2], [N4-R4].

### 5) Climatology improves short-term forecasting methods themselves

Fog climatology does not just support forecasting; it actively enhances the methods used for short-term forecasting. The evidence shows that fog forecasting is carried out by numerical weather prediction (NWP) models or statistical models, and that NWP models forecast the weather based on numerical simulations [N3-R4]. Climatology is therefore useful for initialization because it provides a baseline state that can be used to calibrate models and correct biases [N3-R2]. It also helps with bias correction, as the evidence explicitly states that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2].

This means that climatology provides both the training data and the validation targets needed to build and test forecasting algorithms [N3-F2].

It also notes that FogCast is a Bayesian neural network-based model that forecasts fog using the outputs of GraphCast and accounts for aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties [N5-R1]. The review on fog formation and classification further emphasizes that the complexity in fog forecasting is high due to multiple factors acting at multiple levels, which supports the need for probabilistic approaches [N5-R4]. Together, these sources show that climatology enables forecasting systems to move beyond deterministic predictions toward probabilistic and ensemble methods, which are especially valuable for short-term fog forecasts where uncertainty is high [N3-R3], [N5-R1], [N5-R4].

### 6) Practical limits and research gaps remain

Despite these benefits, fog climatology-based forecasting is not perfect. The evidence indicates that assumptions in climatology may not hold under changing climate or extreme conditions. Fog forecasting is complex because multiple factors play a role at multiple levels, and the complexity is high due to changing climate and environmental conditions [N5-R4]. This means that historical climatological patterns may become less reliable as climate changes, especially if new patterns emerge or existing relationships weaken [N5-R4].

Model resolution and data quality also limit practical implementation. The evidence states that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2]. The climatology evidence further suggests that bias correction and merging datasets with seasonal and annual corrections are needed to improve prediction techniques [N1-R4], showing that data quality is a major practical constraint.

Operational trade-offs exist between accuracy, lead time, and cost. It also notes that many studies still require improvement in forecasting effectiveness and regional specificity, and that a single model is difficult to apply universally because underlying surface characteristics, circulation, and climatic background vary across regions [N3-F2]. At the same time, the climatology literature shows that bias correction and validation with historical data are important for improving forecasts [N3-R2], [N6-R1]. This means that operational systems must balance accuracy against the cost of higher-resolution data, more complex models, and longer lead times, while also accepting that some forecasts will remain uncertain, especially in extreme or changing conditions [N3-F2], [N5-R4].

### Bottom line

Overall, fog climatology analyses enhance short-term airport forecasting by providing the background patterns that make fog more predictable, by identifying the most informative forecasting metrics, by capturing seasonal and diurnal variation, and by improving the methods used to predict fog. This in turn reduces uncertainty in scheduling and delays, supports better resource allocation, and extends the window for runway and operational decisions [N2-R4], [N4-R2], [N1-R3]. At the same time, the evidence also shows that practical limits remain: climatological assumptions may not hold under changing climate or extreme conditions, model resolution and data quality can constrain implementation, and operational systems must balance accuracy, lead time, and cost [N5-R4], [N3-R2], [N3-F2]. In practice, climatology is therefore not a magic bullet, but a powerful tool that makes fog forecasting more reliable, more informative, and more useful for airports.

## How fog climatology analyses enhance short-term airport forecasting

Fog climatology analyses enhance short-term airport forecasting by turning weather uncertainty into actionable information. Rather than treating fog as a random event, climatology provides the background patterns that make fog more predictable: seasonal variation, diurnal variation, and the underlying meteorological conditions that govern fog formation. This is especially important at airports, where fog reduces visibility, disrupts flight operations, and causes delays, cancellations, or diversions [N2-R4]. The evidence also shows that fog is a major obstacle for flight operations, and that fog-related flight delays can severely disrupt schedules [N2-R2], [N2-R3]. By using climatology, airports can forecast fog more accurately, more reliably, and with a longer lead time, which in turn supports better scheduling, resource allocation, and runway decision-making [N4-R2], [N4-R4].

### 1) Climatological analysis provides the most informative metrics for fog forecasting

Climatological analysis identifies the metrics that are most informative for fog forecasting. The evidence points to visibility, humidity, temperature, wind speed, and boundary-layer conditions as central predictors [N3-R5]. It also notes that fog is often detected using satellite and ground observations, with validation and bias correction based on climatological data [N6-R1], [N6-R3]. In practical terms, this means that forecasters do not need to guess what conditions will produce fog; they can instead rely on a set of observable and historically validated climatological indicators.

The climatology literature also emphasizes the importance of high-resolution spatiotemporal analysis. One study shows that diurnal fog occurrence can be studied with high spatiotemporal resolution, and another notes that seasonal fog frequency and timing are important [N1-R1], [N1-R3]. These metrics matter because they capture the conditions that make fog more likely, when it tends to form, and how long it is likely to last. For short-term airport forecasting, this is valuable because fog events are often localized and time-sensitive, and climatological metrics help distinguish “likely fog” from “unlikely fog” before conditions worsen [N1-R3], [N1-R4].

### 2) Seasonal patterns change the likelihood and timing of fog events

Seasonal patterns are a major reason why climatology improves forecasting. The evidence shows that fog frequency is not uniform across the year and that seasonal and annual bias corrections are used to calibrate fog prediction techniques [N1-R4]. The diurnal fog study further notes that fog frequency and timing vary seasonally and that spatiotemporal dynamics are important for understanding climate impacts [N1-F1]. This means that seasonal climatology helps forecasters adjust their expectations for different times of year.

For airport operations, this is important because fog may appear at different times and with different persistence depending on the season. For example, some seasons may favor longer persistence and morning formation, while others may emphasize afternoon development or shorter-lived events [N1-R3], [N1-R4]. Climatological knowledge therefore allows forecasters to tune models and thresholds differently by season, which is especially useful when planning for peak fog periods or unusual seasonal conditions [N1-R3], [N1-R4].

### 3) Diurnal cycles influence fog formation, persistence, and dissipation

Diurnal cycles are another key climatological feature that enhances forecasting. The evidence shows that fog often has a daily pattern: peak occurrence is typically between 06:00 and 10:00 local time, and daily fog persistence can extend for several hours [N1-R3]. The same study notes that fog dynamics are important for energy, nutrient, and hydrological cycles, which reinforces the idea that fog is not just a random weather event but a predictable daily process [N1-F1].

For short-term airport forecasting, this means that diurnal climatology helps forecasters identify when fog is most likely to develop, how long it may persist after formation, and under what conditions it may dissipate. This is especially valuable because airport operations depend on knowing fog onset, duration, and dissipation timing. In practice, diurnal climatology can help forecasters anticipate the morning fog that may delay departures or the afternoon fog that may require runway closures, allowing airports to adjust schedules and operations more effectively [N1-R3], [N1-F1].

### 4) Airport forecasting benefits from improved fog forecasts

The operational benefits of climatological fog knowledge are substantial. The evidence shows that fog forecasts reduce uncertainty in airport scheduling and delays because they improve visibility prediction and allow for better planning [N2-R4]. They also support resource allocation and staffing because fog is not random and can be anticipated seasonally and diurnally [N1-R3]. In practical terms, this means that airports can plan for more staff, equipment, or communication during peak fog periods and allocate resources more efficiently during morning or late-night fog peaks [N1-R3].

Forecast lead time is another critical benefit. The evidence notes that accurate fog forecasts are imperative for aviation to prevent costly delays and diversions [N4-R2]. It also states that early prediction enables timely control measures, while ensemble and probabilistic methods help depict atmospheric conditions more objectively and reduce uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. This matters for airports because longer lead times give more time to delay departures, adjust flight sequences, or delay takeoffs and landings, while shorter lead times force more urgent, real-time decisions [N4-F3]. In short, climatology increases the window for proactive decision-making, which is essential in airport operations where every hour counts [N4-R2], [N4-R4].

### 5) Climatology improves short-term forecasting methods themselves

Fog climatology does not just support forecasting; it actively enhances the methods used for short-term forecasting. The evidence shows that fog forecasting is carried out by numerical weather prediction (NWP) models or statistical models, and that NWP models forecast the weather based on numerical simulations [N3-R4]. Climatology is therefore useful for initialization because it provides a baseline state that can be used to calibrate models and correct biases [N3-R2]. It also helps with bias correction, as the evidence explicitly states that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2].

Climatology also helps train and validate forecasting algorithms. The machine learning-based fog forecasting paper explains that statistical methods use historical data to establish mathematical forecasting models between key meteorological factors and heavy fog weather [N3-F2]. It also notes that numerical model forecasting methods simulate complex interactions and can be used to analyze formation and evolution mechanisms, while dynamic-statistical methods integrate numerical models with statistical methods [N3-F2]. This means that climatology provides both the training data and the validation targets needed to build and test forecasting algorithms [N3-F2].

Finally, climatology supports probabilistic and ensemble forecasting. The evidence highlights that ensemble forecasting is currently pivotal in fog forecasting and offers a more objective depiction of atmospheric conditions while reducing uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. It also notes that FogCast is a Bayesian neural network-based model that forecasts fog using the outputs of GraphCast and accounts for aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties [N5-R1]. The review on fog formation and classification further emphasizes that the complexity in fog forecasting is high due to multiple factors acting at multiple levels, which supports the need for probabilistic approaches [N5-R4]. Together, these sources show that climatology enables forecasting systems to move beyond deterministic predictions toward probabilistic and ensemble methods, which are especially valuable for short-term fog forecasts where uncertainty is high [N3-R3], [N5-R1], [N5-R4].

### 6) Practical limits and research gaps remain

Despite these benefits, fog climatology-based forecasting is not perfect. The evidence indicates that assumptions in climatology may not hold under changing climate or extreme conditions. Fog forecasting is complex because multiple factors play a role at multiple levels, and the complexity is high due to changing climate and environmental conditions [N5-R4]. This means that historical climatological patterns may become less reliable as climate changes, especially if new patterns emerge or existing relationships weaken [N5-R4].

Model resolution and data quality also limit practical implementation. The evidence states that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2]. It also notes that numerical models struggle to meet short-term heavy fog forecasting requirements in terms of accuracy and spatial resolution [N3-F2]. This is important because low-resolution models may miss localized fog formation, while poor-quality input data may produce unreliable forecasts. The climatology evidence further suggests that bias correction and merging datasets with seasonal and annual corrections are needed to improve prediction techniques [N1-R4], showing that data quality is a major practical constraint.

Operational trade-offs exist between accuracy, lead time, and cost. The evidence supports this by showing that ensemble and probabilistic methods improve forecasting by depicting atmospheric conditions more objectively and reducing uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. It also notes that many studies still require improvement in forecasting effectiveness and regional specificity, and that a single model is difficult to apply universally because underlying surface characteristics, circulation, and climatic background vary across regions [N3-F2]. At the same time, the climatology literature shows that bias correction and validation with historical data are important for improving forecasts [N3-R2], [N6-R1]. This means that operational systems must balance accuracy against the cost of higher-resolution data, more complex models, and longer lead times, while also accepting that some forecasts will remain uncertain, especially in extreme or changing conditions [N3-F2], [N5-R4].

### Bottom line

Overall, fog climatology analyses enhance short-term airport forecasting by providing the background patterns that make fog more predictable, by identifying the most informative forecasting metrics, by capturing seasonal and diurnal variation, and by improving the methods used to predict fog. This in turn reduces uncertainty in scheduling and delays, supports better resource allocation, and extends the window for runway and operational decisions [N2-R4], [N4-R2], [N1-R3]. At the same time, the evidence also shows that practical limits remain: climatological assumptions may not hold under changing climate or extreme conditions, model resolution and data quality can constrain implementation, and operational systems must balance accuracy, lead time, and cost [N5-R4], [N3-R2], [N3-F2]. In practice, climatology is therefore not a magic bullet, but a powerful tool that makes fog forecasting more reliable, more informative, and more useful for airports.

Forecast lead time is another critical benefit. The evidence notes that accurate fog forecasts are imperative for aviation to prevent costly delays and diversions [N4-R2]. It also states that early prediction enables timely control measures, while ensemble and probabilistic methods help depict atmospheric conditions more objectively and reduce uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. This matters for airports because longer lead times give more time to delay departures, adjust flight sequences, or delay takeoffs and landings, while shorter lead times force more urgent, real-time decisions [N4-F3]. In short, climatology increases the window for proactive decision-making, which is essential in airport operations where every hour counts [N4-R2], [N4-R4].

### 5) Climatology improves short-term forecasting methods themselves

Fog climatology does not just support forecasting; it actively enhances the methods used for short-term forecasting. The evidence shows that fog forecasting is carried out by numerical weather prediction (NWP) models or statistical models, and that NWP models forecast the weather based on numerical simulations [N3-R4]. Climatology is therefore useful for initialization because it provides a baseline state that can be used to calibrate models and correct biases [N3-R2]. It also helps with bias correction, as the evidence explicitly states that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2].

Climatology also helps train and validate forecasting algorithms. The machine learning-based fog forecasting paper explains that statistical methods use historical data to establish mathematical forecasting models between key meteorological factors and heavy fog weather [N3-F2]. It also notes that numerical model forecasting methods simulate complex interactions and can be used to analyze formation and evolution mechanisms, while dynamic-statistical methods integrate numerical models with statistical methods [N3-F2]. This means that climatology provides both the training data and the validation targets needed to build and test forecasting algorithms [N3-F2].

Finally, climatology supports probabilistic and ensemble forecasting. The evidence highlights that ensemble forecasting is currently pivotal in fog forecasting and offers a more objective depiction of atmospheric conditions while reducing uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. It also notes that FogCast is a Bayesian neural network-based model that forecasts fog using the outputs of GraphCast and accounts for aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties [N5-R1]. The review on fog formation and classification further emphasizes that the complexity in fog forecasting is high due to multiple factors acting at multiple levels, which supports the need for probabilistic approaches [N5-R4]. Together, these sources show that climatology enables forecasting systems to move beyond deterministic predictions toward probabilistic and ensemble methods, which are especially valuable for short-term fog forecasts where uncertainty is high [N3-R3], [N5-R1], [N5-R4].

### 6) Practical limits and research gaps remain

Despite these benefits, fog climatology-based forecasting is not perfect. The evidence indicates that assumptions in climatology may not hold under changing climate or extreme conditions. Fog forecasting is complex because multiple factors play a role at multiple levels, and the complexity is high due to changing climate and environmental conditions [N5-R4]. This means that historical climatological patterns may become less reliable as climate changes, especially if new patterns emerge or existing relationships weaken [N5-R4].

Model resolution and data quality also limit practical implementation. The evidence states that input data from satellite can contain errors that may be corrected with statistical methods such as perfect-prog based on fog climatology and/or ground observations [N3-R2]. It also notes that numerical models struggle to meet short-term heavy fog forecasting requirements in terms of accuracy and spatial resolution [N3-F2]. This is important because low-resolution models may miss localized fog formation, while poor-quality input data may produce unreliable forecasts. The climatology evidence further suggests that bias correction and merging datasets with seasonal and annual corrections are needed to improve prediction techniques [N1-R4], showing that data quality is a major practical constraint.

Operational trade-offs exist between accuracy, lead time, and cost. The evidence supports this by showing that ensemble and probabilistic methods improve forecasting by depicting atmospheric conditions more objectively and reducing uncertainties associated with single forecasts [N3-R3]. It also notes that many studies still require improvement in forecasting effectiveness and regional specificity, and that a single model is difficult to apply universally because underlying surface characteristics, circulation, and climatic background vary across regions [N3-F2]. At the same time, the climatology literature shows that bias correction and validation with historical data are important for improving forecasts [N3-R2], [N6-R1]. This means that operational systems must balance accuracy against the cost of higher-resolution data, more complex models, and longer lead times, while also accepting that some forecasts will remain uncertain, especially in extreme or changing conditions [N3-F2], [N5-R4].

### Bottom line

Overall, fog climatology analyses enhance short-term airport forecasting by providing the background patterns that make fog more predictable, by identifying the most informative forecasting metrics, by capturing seasonal and diurnal variation, and by improving the methods used to predict fog. This in turn reduces uncertainty in scheduling and delays, supports better resource allocation, and extends the window for runway and operational decisions [N2-R4], [N4-R2], [N1-R3]. At the same time, the evidence also shows that practical limits remain: climatological assumptions may not hold under changing climate or extreme conditions, model resolution and data quality can constrain implementation, and operational systems must balance accuracy, lead time, and cost [N5-R4], [N3-R2], [N3-F2]. In practice, climatology is therefore not a magic bullet, but a powerful tool that makes fog forecasting more reliable, more informative, and more useful for airports.
